summary: Provides an overview of the attribute types and object classes defined by ISO and ITU-T in the X.500 documents, especially those intended for directory clients, for use with LDAPv3. It was replaced by several later RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: An LDAP directory stores information as entries, and each entry has named attributes such as a surname or a country code. This document lists the attributes and object classes that come from the X.500 directory standard, written in the form LDAPv3 uses, and says what shape each value takes. It is a reference for anyone building a client or a server against a directory.

subtitle: The X.500 user schema written in LDAPv3 form, so a directory client knows which attributes and object classes exist.

tldr.problem: LDAPv3 gave a way to query a directory, but a client still needed to know which attribute types and object classes it would find there, and in what form each value was written.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC restates the X.500(96) user schema in LDAPv3 notation, listing the attribute types with their syntaxes and matching rules, the object classes with their required and optional attributes, and the value syntaxes themselves.
tldr.outcome: A server that recognises these definitions can answer questions about people, organizations and devices in a predictable shape. RFC 2256 was obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517, RFC 4519 and RFC 4523.

facts.label: objectClass values per entry
facts.value: At least 2, one of them top or alias

today: RFC 2256 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 4510, RFC 4512, RFC 4517, RFC 4519 and RFC 4523. It was updated by RFC 3377.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
This document provides an overview of the attribute types and object classes defined by the ISO and ITU-T committees in the X.500 documents, in particular those intended for use by directory clients. The RFC says this is the most widely used schema for LDAP and X.500 directories, and that many other schema definitions for white pages objects use it as a basis. It does not cover attributes used for the administration of X.500 directory servers, nor does it include attributes defined by other ISO and ITU-T documents.

The definitions are written in the BNF form of AttributeTypeDescription and ObjectClassDescription given in RFC 2252, with lines folded for readability. The schema definitions are based on those found in the X.500 documents X.501, X.509, X.520 and X.521 and their updates, together with RFC 1274 for a few syntaxes and object classes. Some attribute names differ from those found in X.520(93), and three new attributes, supportedAlgorithms, deltaRevocationList and dmdName, and the objectClass dmd, are defined in the X.500(96) documents.

The document carries an IESG note. LDAPv3 provides both read and update access, and update access requires secure authentication, but this document does not mandate any satisfactory authentication mechanism. It was approved as a Proposed Standard despite that limitation, to encourage implementation and interoperability testing, to encourage deployment in read-only applications, and to avoid delaying other standards-track protocols that need to query but not update LDAPv3 servers. Readers are warned that until mandatory authentication mechanisms are standardised, clients and servers written to this specification which use update functionality are unlikely to interoperate, or may interoperate only if authentication is reduced to an unacceptably weak level, and implementors are discouraged from deploying such clients or servers until a Proposed Standard for mandatory authentication in LDAPv3 has been published as an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a reference list, not a protocol. It says which attributes a directory entry can carry, what each one means, and what object classes group them. The IESG note warns that reading a directory was settled but writing to one was not, because no mandatory authentication had been agreed, so updates were not safe to depend on.

sections.title: Attribute Types
sections.content:
An LDAP server implementation SHOULD recognise the attribute types described in this section. Each definition gives the attribute's object identifier, its name, the rule used to compare two values for equality, the rule used to match substrings where one is given, the syntax of its values and any size limit, and whether it is single valued.

Some attributes are structural. The objectClass attribute describes the kind of object an entry represents and is present in every entry with at least two values, one of which is either top or alias. The aliasedObjectName attribute is used by the directory service when the entry is an alias. The knowledgeInformation attribute is no longer used.

Several attributes are short forms of a longer X.500 name. cn is the commonName attribute, which contains a name of an object and is typically a person's full name. sn is the surname attribute. c holds a two-letter ISO 3166 country code and is single valued. l holds the name of a locality such as a city or county, st the full name of a state or province, street the physical address of the object, o the name of an organization and ou the name of an organizational unit. title holds the title of a person in their organizational context, such as "Vice President", where personalTitle would be used for a title independent of the job function. description holds a human-readable description, and businessCategory describes the kind of business an organization performs.

A group of attributes is used for certificates and keys. userCertificate, cACertificate, authorityRevocationList, certificateRevocationList and crossCertificatePair are all stored and requested in binary form, with the name ending in ;binary. userPassword is stored using an Octet String syntax and is not encrypted, so the transfer of cleartext passwords is strongly discouraged where the underlying transport cannot guarantee confidentiality.

The name attribute type is the supertype from which string attribute types typically used for naming may be formed, and it is unlikely that values of it occur in an entry. Client implementations MUST NOT assume that LDAP servers are capable of performing attribute subtyping. givenName holds the part of a person's name that is neither surname nor middle name, initials the initials of some or all of an individual's names but not the surnames, and generationQualifier the suffix part of a name. x500UniqueIdentifier is used to distinguish objects when a distinguished name has been reused, and is a different attribute type from both the uid and uniqueIdentifier types. dnQualifier carries disambiguating information to add to the relative distinguished name of an entry, intended for use when merging data from multiple sources to prevent conflicts between entries that would otherwise have the same name. The searchGuide attribute is for X.500 clients constructing search filters and is obsoleted by enhancedSearchGuide.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute gets a number, a name, and a rule for how its values are compared. The common ones are short: cn for a common name, sn for a surname, c for a country code, l for a locality, st for a state, o for an organization and ou for a unit. Certificates are held in binary form under names ending in ;binary, and the password attribute holds an unencrypted octet string, which is why the RFC warns against sending passwords in the clear.

sections.title: Syntaxes
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD recognise the syntaxes defined in this section. Each syntax begins with a sample value of the ldapSyntaxes attribute, which defines the object identifier of the syntax. The descriptions of syntax names are not carried in the protocol and are not guaranteed to be unique.

The Delivery Method syntax describes how a message is delivered, with values built from the production delivery-value = pdm / ( pdm whsp "$" whsp delivery-value ) and the pdm production listing any, mhs, physical, telex, teletex, g3fax, g4fax, ia5, videotex and telephone. The example given is telephone.

The Enhanced Guide syntax was added after RFC 1778 and is written as EnhancedGuide = woid whsp "#" whsp criteria whsp "#" whsp subset, where the subset is baseobject, oneLevel or wholeSubtree. The example is person#(sn)#oneLevel. The Guide syntax it builds on is guide-value = [ object-class "#" ] criteria, where a criteria set combines criteria with & or |, a criteria item is an attribute type paired with a match type of EQ, SUBSTR, GE, LE or APPROX, and a criteria item may be negated with a leading !. The RFC states that this syntax should not be used for defining new attributes.

The remaining syntaxes are Octet String, which carries values as octet strings, with the example secret; the Teletex Terminal Identifier, written as a printable string followed by any number of $-separated parameters whose keys are graphic, control, misc, page or private; and the Telex Number, written as an actual number, a country and an answerback code separated by $. The Supported Algorithm syntax has no printable representation defined in this document, so clients that wish to store and retrieve the supportedAlgorithms attribute MUST use supportedAlgorithms;binary, with the value transferred as a binary encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: A syntax says what shape a value has, so the server knows how to compare it and how to send it. Most are text with a fixed grammar, such as a delivery method or a telex number. The supported algorithm syntax has no printable form at all, so it is transferred as raw bytes with a ;binary suffix.

sections.title: Object Classes
sections.content:
LDAP servers MUST recognise the object classes top and subschema, and SHOULD recognise all the other object classes listed as values of the objectClass attribute.

The class top is abstract and is the superclass of everything else. alias extends it and MUST have an aliasedObjectName. country MUST have a c and MAY have a searchGuide and a description. locality MAY have street, seeAlso, searchGuide, st, l and description. organization MUST have an o and MAY have a long list including userPassword, businessCategory, postalAddress, telephoneNumber, facsimileTelephoneNumber, st, l and description; organizationalUnit is the same shape but MUST have an ou instead.

person MUST have both a sn and a cn, and MAY have a userPassword, telephoneNumber, seeAlso and description. organizationalPerson extends person and adds a title, postal and telephone attributes, and organizational unit, state and locality. organizationalRole MUST have a cn and MAY have a roleOccupant and an owner. groupOfNames MUST have a member and a cn, and groupOfUniqueNames MUST have a uniqueMember and a cn. residentialPerson extends person and MUST have an l.

Several classes exist for devices and applications. applicationProcess MUST have a cn, applicationEntity MUST have a presentationAddress and a cn, dSA extends applicationEntity and MAY have the old knowledgeInformation attribute, and device MUST have a cn and MAY have a serialNumber, owner, organizational unit, organization, locality and description. strongAuthenticationUser and certificationAuthority are auxiliary classes that MUST have a userCertificate and MUST have the revocation lists and CA certificate respectively. userSecurityInformation is auxiliary and MAY have supportedAlgorithms. certificationAuthority-V2 extends certificationAuthority as an auxiliary class and MAY have a deltaRevocationList, and cRLDistributionPoint MUST have a cn and MAY have the certificate, authority and delta revocation lists. Finally dmd MUST have a dmdName.
sections.plainLanguage: An object class says what kind of thing an entry is and therefore which attributes it must have. A person must have a surname and a common name. An organization must have an organization name. A group of names must have its members listed. Every class sits under the abstract class top, so a client can ask for any object class and get everything that inherits from it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attributes of directory entries are used to provide descriptive information about the real-world objects they represent, which can be people, organizations or devices. Most countries have privacy laws regarding the publication of information about people.

The transfer of cleartext passwords is strongly discouraged where the underlying transport service cannot guarantee confidentiality, and may result in disclosure of the password to unauthorized parties. This matches the note on the userPassword attribute itself, which records that passwords are stored using an Octet String syntax and are not encrypted.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory entries describe real people and organisations, and most countries have privacy laws about publishing information about people. The other warning is practical: the password attribute is not encrypted, so sending it over a link that does not protect its contents can disclose it.

cells: The kind of object the entry represents. Every entry has at least two values, one of them top or alias.
The common name of the object, typically a person's full name.

The full name of a state or province.

viz.caption: THE SYNTAXES DEFINED IN RFC 2256 SECTION 6

items.label: Delivery Method
items.desc: How a message is delivered, such as telephone or telex.

items.label: Enhanced Guide
items.desc: A search guide written as object, criteria and subset.

items.label: Guide
items.desc: The older search guide syntax, which should not be used for new attributes.

items.label: Supported Algorithm
items.desc: No printable form is defined, so it is transferred as binary.

items.label: Teletex Terminal Identifier
items.desc: A terminal identifier with optional parameters.

items.label: Telex Number
items.desc: An actual number, a country and an answerback code.

viz.caption: THE OBJECT CLASSES A DIRECTORY ENTRY COMMONLY USES

items.title: top
items.text: The abstract superclass every other class derives from.

items.title: person
items.text: Must have a surname and a common name.

items.title: organizationalPerson
items.text: A person in an organizational context. It extends person.

items.title: organizationalUnit
items.text: Must have the organizational unit name.

items.title: groupOfNames
items.text: Must have a member list and a common name.

items.title: device
items.text: Must have a common name, and may have a serial number.
